strengths: The paper identifies a clear and relevant problem for VLA policies: intermediate reasoning in language or image space can be poorly aligned with low-level control. The proposed action-space reasoning framing is intuitive and technically plausible.

The method is concrete and reasonably well motivated: EAR produces coarse reference trajectories, IAR extracts latent action priors from VLM KV caches, and AGP uses cross-attention to condition the final action denoising head. This is a coherent extension of flow/action-generation policies rather than just a conceptual rebranding.

Empirical coverage is fairly broad. The paper evaluates on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, VLABench, and real robots, with especially strong gains on LIBERO-Plus robustness perturbations over a pi0.5 baseline: 75.7% to 84.1% average success.

The ablations are useful. EAR and IAR are evaluated separately and jointly, KV-cache interaction alternatives are compared, reference action horizons/shifts are varied, and latency/parameter overhead is reported. These support the claim that the gains are not solely from naive scaling.
The real-world experiments, while limited, add practical evidence across contact-rich wiping, pouring, open-set picking, and a second embodiment for open-set pick.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is somewhat overstated. EAR is close to an auxiliary trajectory predictor/self-conditioning module for a diffusion or flow policy, and IAR is an attention pooling mechanism over VLM features. The “Action Chain-of-Thought” terminology is rhetorically appealing but the paper does not establish a deeper reasoning process beyond learned action-space conditioning.

The strongest simulation benchmark, LIBERO, is highly saturated: the absolute average gain over strong baselines is small, e.g. 96.9% to 98.5% over pi0.5. The more meaningful gains are on LIBERO-Plus, but several compared methods appear to be taken from different sources or reproduced selectively, and full fairness across training budgets, model sizes, data, and implementations is not always clear.

VLABench results are mixed. The method improves average intention/progress scores, but it underperforms pi0.5 on commonsense and semantic-instruction intention scores. This weakens the broad claim that action-space reasoning uniformly improves generalization and reasoning.

The real-world evaluation has small trial counts and no statistical uncertainty. For example, Pour Water remains low at 33.3%, and average real-world success is 66.7%. The reported improvements are promising but not decisive without confidence intervals, repeated seeds, or more tasks.

There is a potentially important train-test mismatch: during training, Zex is computed from ground-truth reference trajectories via teacher forcing, while inference relies on EAR predictions. The paper acknowledges stabilization but does not quantify the quality of EAR trajectories, compounding errors, or sensitivity to inaccurate reference actions.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Important implementation details are underspecified, including exact flow-matching parameterization/noise schedule, action normalization, architecture widths for EAR/action head beyond parameter counts, decoding/denoising settings, and data preprocessing. The learning-rate description also appears inconsistent, stating a peak of 5e-5 and decay toward 5e-5.

The paper would benefit from deeper diagnostics showing why the generated reference actions help: trajectory visualizations, EAR prediction accuracy, failure cases where EAR misleads the action head, and comparisons to simpler auxiliary losses or action-token conditioning baselines.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem in VLA robot policies: reducing the mismatch between high-level multimodal representations and low-level action prediction.

The proposed architecture is concrete and reasonably motivated: an Explicit Action Reasoner predicts coarse reference trajectories, while an Implicit Action Reasoner extracts action-related priors from VLM key-value caches, and both are fused by cross-attention in the action head.

The simulation evaluation is broad, covering LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and VLABench, and the ablations generally support that EAR and IAR improve over the authors' pi0.5-style baseline, especially on LIBERO-Plus robustness settings.
The appendix adds useful implementation and dataset details, including action spaces, horizons, training steps, batch size, and latency/parameter tradeoffs.
weaknesses: The main novelty is overstated. Despite the Action Chain-of-Thought framing, the method is essentially auxiliary action-trajectory self-conditioning plus latent feature cross-attention. The paper does not convincingly distinguish this from standard action priors, hierarchical/action-chunk prediction, or self-conditioning beyond terminology.

The evidence for the central claim that the model 'reasons' in action space is weak. There is no analysis of the generated reference trajectories, their accuracy, failure cases, interpretability, or whether the action intermediate is causally useful beyond acting as an extra learned module with more parameters.

Some claims are not supported by the reported results. In the real-world plot, ACoT-VLA appears worse than pi0.5 on the AgiBot G1 open-set pick task, yet the text says it is consistently higher than both pi0.5 and pi0. This undermines confidence in the experimental interpretation.

The real-world evaluation is quite small and noisy: only 24 trials for wipe stain, 12 for pour water, and 40 for open-set pick according to the appendix, with no confidence intervals or significance tests. The reported 66.7% average success rate is modest, and task-level gains are mixed.

Fairness of the large comparison tables is unclear. Many baselines are taken from heterogeneous sources, while only some are reproduced. Differences in backbone, data, training budget, input state, and evaluation protocol may explain part of the gains, especially on saturated LIBERO where the absolute improvement over prior best is small.

The train-test mismatch introduced by teacher forcing is a material concern: during training the action head receives embeddings from ground-truth reference trajectories, while at inference it receives EAR predictions. The paper does not quantify exposure bias or compare against alternatives such as scheduled sampling or predicted-reference training.

Reproducibility is incomplete for a CVPR-level robotics paper. Important details such as exact architecture dimensions for EAR/action head variants, flow-matching parameterization, normalization, action preprocessing, random seeds, checkpoint selection, and code availability are missing or underspecified.

Presentation quality is uneven, with grammatical issues and some confusing details, e.g. the learning-rate schedule says it decays from 5e-5 toward 5e-5. These are not the main reason for rejection, but they add friction and occasionally obscure technical correctness.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and useful idea: shifting intermediate reasoning for VLA policies from language/vision space into action space. The Explicit Action Reasoner and Implicit Action Reasoner are well motivated, fit naturally with flow-matching action heads, and provide a plausible mechanism for reducing the semantic-to-kinematic gap.

The empirical evaluation is broad for this area. The method is tested on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, VLABench, and real robots, with especially convincing gains on LIBERO-Plus robustness settings (75.7% to 84.1% over the pi0.5 baseline) and consistent improvements in most simulation benchmarks.

The ablation studies are meaningful. The paper separately evaluates EAR and IAR, reference action horizon/shift, KV-cache interaction designs, parameter/denoising budget controls, and latency. These experiments support the claim that the gains are not merely due to a larger action head or more denoising steps.

The method has practical appeal: IAR adds little latency, and the combined model reports a moderate latency increase from 91 ms to 112 ms while improving success rates substantially on the harder benchmark.
The manuscript is generally readable, with a coherent method description and useful appendix details on datasets, training configurations, and real-world evaluation protocols.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is somewhat overstated. EAR resembles action-space self-conditioning or hierarchical trajectory proposal mechanisms, and the paper would benefit from a sharper distinction from prior self-conditioning, action-chunking, and plan-conditioned policies beyond framing it as Action Chain-of-Thought.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence. LIBERO is nearly saturated, so the 96.9% to 98.5% gain is useful but small; the strongest case comes from LIBERO-Plus. The paper repeatedly claims state-of-the-art performance, but not all baselines appear to be reproduced under matched conditions, and the comparison mixes published numbers with reproduced results.

The real-world evaluation is encouraging but limited. Trial counts are small for several tasks, success is operator assessed, and no confidence intervals or repeated-seed statistics are reported. In Fig. 4, the AgiBot open-set pick result appears lower than pi0.5 despite the text suggesting consistently higher performance, which weakens the real-world generality claim.

The training/inference mismatch for EAR is a material concern. During training, Zex is computed from ground-truth reference trajectories, while inference uses EAR-generated references. The paper reports strong results, but it does not deeply analyze error propagation, reference trajectory quality, or cases where EAR misguides the action head.

Reproducibility is only partial. The paper provides many hyperparameters and dataset statistics, but lacks details such as random seeds, variance across runs, precise baseline reproduction settings, code/model release plans, and some implementation specifics needed to reproduce the full system reliably.

The limitations section is relatively brief and does not fully address potential failure modes, such as low success on Pour Water, sensitivity to action representation choices, robustness to poor EAR predictions, or whether the approach transfers to substantially different control frequencies and embodiments.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and potentially useful idea: providing intermediate guidance directly in action space rather than only through language or visual subgoals. The Explicit Action Reasoner and Implicit Action Reasoner are natural, technically plausible modules for this goal.

The empirical section is broad: results are reported on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, VLABench, real-world AgiBot G1 tasks, cross-embodiment Open-set Pick, and Genie-Sim sim-to-real transfer. This is stronger evidence than a single benchmark improvement.

Ablations support the main design choices. EAR and IAR each improve over the pi0.5 baseline, their combination performs best, and the appendix studies reference horizon/shift, KV-cache interaction variants, parameter scale, denoising budget, latency, and sim-to-real transfer.

The method appears practically useful: the strongest version improves LIBERO-Plus supervised fine-tuning from 75.7% to 88.0%, zero-shot LIBERO-Plus from 85.7% to 86.6%, and VLABench average scores over pi0.5, while adding moderate latency according to the reported measurements.

The manuscript is mostly well structured and easy to follow, with a coherent motivation around the semantic-kinematic gap and a reasonably complete description of the architecture and training objective.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is somewhat overstated. EAR resembles an auxiliary action predictor/self-conditioning mechanism trained on the same action supervision, and the paper does not fully distinguish ACoT from prior hierarchical action planning, diffusion self-conditioning, action chunking, or latent action approaches beyond terminology.

The training-inference mismatch is a material concern: during training, the action head receives Z_ex computed from ground-truth reference trajectories, while at inference it receives EAR-generated references. The paper mentions this stabilization but does not quantify exposure-bias effects, reference-trajectory quality, or how often poor EAR predictions mislead the final policy.

Some comparisons are hard to interpret. Many Table 1 baselines appear drawn from heterogeneous papers with different backbones, data, evaluation details, and training budgets, while the proposed method is built on pi0.5. The most controlled comparisons are stronger, but the headline state-of-the-art table may overclaim fairness.

The gains on saturated benchmarks are modest in some settings, e.g. LIBERO average improves from 96.9 to 98.5, and VLABench improvements are mixed across tracks, with commonsense IS/PS lower than pi0.5. The paper would benefit from deeper analysis of when action-space guidance fails.

The real-world evaluation is valuable but statistically limited. The appendix describes small trial counts for several tasks, no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported, and the datasets are private, making the 66.7% vs 61.0% improvement difficult to judge robustly.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The abstract contains an unfinished code link, real-world data are custom-collected, and several implementation details remain underspecified, such as exact compute cost for training, parameter allocation, loss/noise schedules, and complete inference procedure.

There are presentation and polish issues that slightly reduce confidence: duplicated rows in Table 10, a likely typo in the learning-rate schedule saying decay from 5e-5 toward 5e-5, crowded tables, and occasional grammatical errors. These are not fatal but should be corrected.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem in VLA robot policies: how to provide action-level guidance rather than relying only on semantic or visual intermediate representations.

The proposed architecture is concrete and reasonably simple: an Explicit Action Reasoner generates coarse reference trajectories, while an Implicit Action Reasoner extracts action-related priors from VLM key/value caches and conditions the final action head.

The evaluation covers several settings, including LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, VLABench, additional ablations, latency analysis, and some real-world robot experiments. The ablations suggest both EAR and IAR contribute measurable gains over the pi0.5-based baseline.

The strongest empirical evidence is on LIBERO-Plus, where the supervised fine-tuning setting improves from 75.7 to 88.0 average success rate, and the frozen-backbone ablation still shows a gain from 75.7 to 84.1.
weaknesses: The central conceptual claim is overstated. The method is presented as a new action chain-of-thought paradigm, but technically it is closer to auxiliary trajectory prediction/self-conditioning plus attention-based feature extraction. The paper does not establish that the generated reference actions constitute interpretable or deliberative reasoning rather than an additional learned action prior.

There is a serious train-test mismatch in the use of EAR: during training, the action head is conditioned on embeddings from ground-truth reference trajectories, while at inference it is conditioned on EAR predictions. The paper acknowledges this teacher-forcing stabilization but does not quantify reference trajectory quality, exposure bias, or failure cases caused by incorrect references.

The comparisons are not fully convincing. Many results in Table 1 are taken from heterogeneous prior works, while the proposed method is built on pi0.5 and may differ in data, compute, tuning, and evaluation details. On the saturated LIBERO benchmark the main gain over pi0.5 is small, 96.9 to 98.5, and no confidence intervals or repeated-run variance are provided.

The real-world evidence is too limited for the strength of the claims. The reported aggregate success rate is 66.7 versus 61.0 for pi0.5, but the appendix describes small evaluation counts for some tasks, e.g. 24 wipe trials and 40 open-set pick trials, and the main paper does not provide per-task statistical uncertainty or detailed failure analysis.

Reproducibility is weak. The abstract says code is available at an incomplete URL, only 'https://github.com/'. The real-world datasets are custom-collected, and important implementation details are underspecified, such as exact action normalization, flow-matching noise schedule, EAR/reference target construction, and how baselines were trained or selected.

The method adds nontrivial cost: Table 12 reports parameter count increasing from 3.35B to 3.81B and latency from 91 ms to 112 ms. The appendix includes some scaling controls, but the main comparisons do not convincingly separate the benefit of the proposed reasoning formulation from added capacity and extra denoising computation.

Some experimental claims are broader than the evidence supports. For example, the paper claims state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks, but VLABench comparisons are only against pi0 and pi0.5 under the authors' setup, and several benchmark tracks show mixed behavior, such as lower commonsense IS/PS than pi0.5 in Table 3.

The presentation has notable polish and clarity issues: several tables are hard to parse, one row in Table 10 is duplicated, the learning-rate schedule description says the peak and final learning rate are both 5e-5, and the paper often uses strong language such as 'paradigm shift' and 'fundamental gap' without equally strong supporting analysis.

strengths: The central idea is useful and well motivated: conditioning VLA policies on action-space intermediate representations directly addresses the semantic-kinematic gap that language or visual subgoals only indirectly handle.

The proposed architecture is technically plausible and concrete. EAR provides coarse reference trajectories, IAR extracts latent action priors from VLM caches, and AGP integrates both via cross-attention in a way that fits modern flow/diffusion action heads.

The empirical support is broad. The paper reports results on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, VLABench, Genie-Sim sim-to-real, and real robot tasks, with consistent gains over the pi0.5 baseline and strong performance under distribution shifts.

The ablations are meaningful: EAR and IAR are tested separately and jointly; the paper studies reference-action horizon/shift, KV-cache interaction strategies, parameter/denoising controls, and latency, which strengthens the causal case for the modules.

The method appears practically relevant: latency increases from 91 ms to 112 ms while improving LIBERO-Plus average success from 75.7 to 84.1 in the reported setting, suggesting a reasonable performance-efficiency tradeoff.
weaknesses: The novelty is somewhat overstated by the Chain-of-Thought framing. EAR is close in spirit to self-conditioning or an auxiliary trajectory predictor, and the paper could more sharply distinguish its contribution from prior action-token, latent-action, and planning-conditioned VLA methods.

Several headline improvements are on saturated benchmarks. On LIBERO, the gain over pi0.5 is modest in absolute terms, so the stronger acceptance case rests mainly on LIBERO-Plus, VLABench, and real-world results.

The real-world evaluation is encouraging but limited. Trial counts are relatively small for some tasks, success criteria involve operator judgment, and no confidence intervals or variance estimates are provided, making it hard to assess statistical reliability.

Reproducibility is incomplete from the manuscript alone. The code link appears unfinished, real-world datasets are private, and many comparisons rely on reported or reproduced checkpoints with potentially different training data, backbones, and tuning budgets.

The training-inference mismatch for EAR deserves deeper analysis: during training the action head receives embeddings from ground-truth reference trajectories, while at inference it depends on EAR-generated references. The paper does not quantify reference trajectory quality or failure modes when EAR is wrong.

Some experimental claims are stronger than the evidence supports. For example, attributing sim-to-real gains specifically to kinematically invariant action guidance is plausible, but the paper does not isolate this mechanism beyond aggregate success rates.

Presentation is generally clear, but some details are confusing or under-specified, such as the learning-rate schedule description, duplicate table rows in the appendix, and exact fairness of parameter-matched comparisons.
